9-1.question: You are building a Bamboo flush around {{s3}}, {{s4}} and {{s5}}. Which tile is the best turn-one decoy to make opponents think Bamboo is dead to you?
options: s9
s4
s5
m2
9-1.explanation: {{s9}} is spare Bamboo, so throwing it early sells the false signal without touching the run you actually need.

9-1.question: What does a successful decoy discard actually buy you? (Select all that apply)
options: Opponents treat your real suit as safe and throw it to you
You get claim chances on the tiles you need
A guaranteed win in that round
Extra faan on the scoring table
Protection from being robbed on a kong
9-1.explanation: A bluff only changes what opponents believe is safe, which creates claim chances but guarantees no win and scores nothing by itself.

9-1.question: Match each discard pattern to the deception or intent it suggests.

pairs.left: One Bamboo on turn 1, then never again
Discards look too tidy for the story they tell
Throws only tiles already seen on the table

9-1.explanation: Each pattern is read from the information the player releases, so an unusually clean story is itself a warning sign.

9-1.question: Early discards are the strongest signal because players throw the tiles they are sure they will ___ need.
9-1.explanation: Players shed what they are certain is useless first, so a turn-one discard is read as real information about their hand.

9-1.question: An opponent's discards look almost too perfect for the flush they seem to be abandoning. What does the lesson advise?
options: Trust the pattern completely
Question the pattern, because it may be a counter-bluff
Ignore all of their discards
Assume they have no plan at all
9-1.explanation: Experienced players treat a suspiciously clean discard pattern as possible deception rather than proof.

9-2.question: You declare a concealed kong of {{m5}} while the rest of your hand is untouched. What happens to 門前清?
options: It is lost, like any kong
It is kept, because a concealed kong does not break it
It is upgraded to 3 faan
It is kept only if you win by self-draw
9-2.explanation: Only a claimed chow, pong or exposed kong breaks 門前清, so a concealed kong leaves the 1 faan intact.

9-2.question: Which kong statements are correct under these rules? (Select all that apply)
options: A kong by itself scores no faan
Robbing a kong (搶槓) scores 1 faan
Every kong breaks 門前清
Each kong adds 1 faan to the hand
A kong self-draw (槓上自摸) scores 1 faan
9-2.explanation: Kongs are not a scoring pattern on their own; only 搶槓 and 槓上自摸 add 1 faan, and a concealed kong keeps 門前清.

9-2.question: Match each kong type to what it costs you or exposes.

pairs.right: Stays face-down and keeps 門前清
Can be robbed for 搶槓
Claimed from a discard, breaking 門前清

9-2.explanation: Whether a kong is claimed is exactly what decides if it leaks information, invites a rob and kills 門前清.

9-2.question: You kong all four copies of {{m5}}. How many copies are left for opponents to use in a chow or pong?
9-2.explanation: Only four copies of a tile exist, so a kong of all four removes that tile from everyone else's options.

9-2.question: You have konged all four {{m8}} and two {{red}} have already been discarded. Order these tiles by copies still unaccounted for, fewest first: {{m8}}, {{red}}, {{p3}}.
9-2.explanation: All four {{m8}} are accounted for, two {{red}} are gone so two remain, and no {{p3}} has been seen so four remain.

9-3.question: Match each playing style to the tell that gives it away.

pairs.right: Calls Pong or Chow on the first tile offered
Stays concealed and builds one big hand
Rebuilds the plan around each starting hand
Throws only tiles already proved safe

9-3.explanation: Style shows up in how quickly a player claims and how long they stay concealed, which is what you profile.

9-3.question: Which of these are fair evidence for profiling an opponent? (Select all that apply)
options: How quickly they claim melds when a tile is offered
Whether they keep the hand concealed deep into the round
How many flowers they were dealt
Their behaviour in the previous round only
9-3.explanation: Style is visible in claiming and concealing, while flowers say nothing about hand shape and last round's behaviour can be stale.

9-3.question: A player who changes plan to suit each starting hand is described as ___.
9-3.explanation: That flexibility is the defining trait of the adaptive profile, which makes them the hardest to read.

9-3.question: An opponent who had been calling melds all round suddenly stops and throws only seen tiles. What should your read be based on?
options: Their play from the first two rounds
Their pattern within the current round
Their seat position
Their total score
9-3.explanation: Against an adaptive player the current round's discards carry the information, not the history you already profiled.

9-3.question: Why is a conservative player most dangerous late in the round?
options: They always hold a limit hand
Their hand is still hidden, so you cannot read their wait
They discard more tiles than anyone else
They win ties against aggressive players
9-3.explanation: A player who never claims reveals almost nothing, so by the late round you still cannot tell which tiles they need.

9-4.question: Which situations call for deliberately slowing the game? (Select all that apply)
options: You are ahead on points and a draw keeps your lead
An opponent looks close to a hand you cannot defend against
You are one tile from winning
You are behind and must catch up
9-4.explanation: Slowing protects a lead and starves a dangerous hand, while being close to winning or far behind both call for speed.

9-4.question: Every claim replaces one of your draws. If you claim three melds, how many fewer draws do you personally take from the wall?
9-4.explanation: A chow or pong is taken instead of a draw, so three claims cost you three draws and shorten the round.

9-4.question: Match each table read to the pace decision it calls for.

pairs.left: A cheap win is one meld away
pairs.right: Claim the meld and close the round

pairs.left: Your hand still needs several tiles
You lead and the wall is thin
pairs.right: Let the round die on a draw

9-4.explanation: Pace follows what each outcome is worth to you, so the same wall can be raced or starved.

9-4.question: Why exactly does claiming a discard shorten the round?
options: It burns one of your flowers
You take the discard instead of drawing, so the wall empties sooner
It forces the dealer to pay
It removes the claimed tile from the wall
9-4.explanation: A claim uses an opponent's discard rather than a fresh wall tile, so fewer draws remain in the round.

9-4.question: The wall runs out with no winner. What happens to the dealer?
options: The dealer repeats as dealer
There is no repeat, so the deal passes on
The dealer pays every other player
The dealer draws one extra tile to settle it
9-4.explanation: A drawn round is not a dealer repeat under these rules, so no 連莊 follows.

9-5.question: You hold Bamboo and honour tiles and want 混一色 for 3 faan. Which of these tiles must stay out of the hand?
options: p5
s5
east
red
9-5.explanation: 混一色 allows one suit plus honour tiles only, so any Circle tile breaks it.

9-5.question: You must discard to an opponent who threw {{m4}} this round and has not drawn since, threw {{p8}} last round, and has never seen {{s6}}. Order the three from safest to most dangerous.
9-5.explanation: A tile they discarded this round before drawing again is absolutely safe, one from an earlier round only relatively safe, and an unseen tile is unread.

9-5.question: Match each stage 9 tactic to what it is for.

pairs.right: Selling a suit you do not actually want
Choosing when to take the replacement draw
Ending the round before rivals improve
Predicting which hand an opponent is building

9-5.explanation: Deception, kong timing, tempo and profiling are four levers on the same information the table shares.

9-5.question: Which statements are true under these rules? (Select all that apply)
options: A hand must reach 3 faan to win
A concealed kong does not break 門前清
Being robbed on a kong is paid by the robbed player alone, as 包自摸
The dealer receives a 50% bonus when winning
Each extra faan doubles the payment
9-5.explanation: There is no dealer bonus and payments step 8, 16, 24, 32 rather than doubling, while the other three match the rules reference.

9-5.question: You lead by 60 points with six wall tiles left and an opponent has three exposed melds. What is the best play?
options: Claim any meld to finish first
Kong for extra replacement draws
Fold, stop claiming, and let the wall run out
Throw middle tiles to bait a claim
9-5.explanation: A draw preserves the lead, and every claim would hand a dangerous opponent more turns before the wall dies.
